rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window. This should reveal whether any peaks are unretained, held to the final hold, or missing, guiding tighter follow-up gradients.

All 10 peaks eluted well within the gradient, so tighten the phi window to bracket the observed elution range and improve time efficiency while keeping similar slope. This tests whether the whole mixture can be focused into a lower-organic window without losing resolution or pushing late peaks into the hold.

The broad window at 20 min already gave perfect resolution term, so now test a steeper gradient to cut run time and see how sensitive the closest mid-run pairs are to slope. This will show whether CRF can be improved mainly by shortening tG without sacrificing critical resolution.

The 10 min run is fast but over-compresses the critical cluster around peaks 5–7, while 20 min resolved it well; an intermediate tG should recover most of that selectivity with little or no time penalty in the CRF. This directly probes the slope sensitivity of the worst pair to find the shortest acceptable gradient.

The critical pair improves strongly with shallower slope, and 14 min is close but still below 1.5 for peaks 6–7. A small increase to 16 min should push that pair into acceptable resolution while likely keeping the time penalty at zero, potentially maximizing CRF.

The critical 6–7 pair appears near the threshold where a modest temperature shift could improve selectivity without needing the longer 16 min program. Testing a 5 C lower temperature at the current best tG probes whether temperature can separate that pair enough to beat the 14 min, 40 C method.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by changing which pair is critical, so now test the opposite direction. A 5 C increase may improve the crowded mid-cluster selectivity at the same short gradient and could outperform the current best without adding time penalty.

Temperature shifts both directions hurt, so slope is the cleaner lever; with 14 min slightly under-resolving and 16 min incurring a small time penalty, 12 min brackets the response curve on the fast side. This helps confirm whether the CRF maximum is truly near 14 min or whether the scoring favors an even shorter run despite lower minimum resolution.

All compounds elute by 9.4 min and the estimated elution window stays well below the top of the current gradient, so trimming phi1 slightly may improve effective selectivity in the crowded middle without extending the run much. This tests whether the critical pair depends not just on slope but on the absolute phi window.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical pair and the CRF, so continue trimming the upper end of the gradient window while all peaks still elute comfortably within the gradient. This should show whether the optimum lies at an even narrower high-organic limit before the last compound begins to crowd the hold.

The best region is now around phi1 = 0.90, and the main tradeoff is between a slightly under-resolved critical pair and total time. Combining the improved phi window with a somewhat steeper 12 min gradient tests whether the CRF peak is dominated by the narrowed window or still requires the 14 min slope.

At phi1 = 0.90, the 14 min method is very close to ideal but the critical pair still sits slightly below 1.5, so a 16 min version should clarify whether the narrowed window can reach full resolution with only a small time cost. This directly tests whether phi1 = 0.90 can surpass the current best by improving the resolution term more than the time term worsens.

With phi1 = 0.90, slope appears near-optimal, so the remaining opportunity is a small selectivity gain from temperature at the narrowed window rather than the broad one. Testing 35 C checks whether the changed phi window alters the temperature response of the critical cluster enough to improve on the current best.

At phi1 = 0.90, lowering temperature again hurt by collapsing peaks 5–6, so test the opposite temperature direction once at the narrowed window to complete the selectivity map. If 45 C also worsens the critical cluster, we can confidently focus remaining injections on fine phi-window tuning around 40 C.

Temperature is clearly not the winning lever, so continue optimizing the gradient window at 40 C. Since phi1 = 0.85 gave full resolution but a slight time penalty and phi1 = 0.90 gave the best CRF, testing phi1 = 0.80 will show whether a still narrower window improves selectivity enough to offset any extra retention.

The optimum seems centered near phi1 = 0.90, so now test whether lifting phi0 slightly while keeping the same upper bound sharpens the crowded mid-elution region and trims unnecessary low-organic dwell. This probes absolute window placement, not just width, which may improve the critical pair without much time cost.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved both time and the critical pair, so combine that gain with the earlier observation that a slightly lower phi1 can further enhance selectivity. This is the most promising neighboring condition for potentially pushing the critical pair above 1.5 while keeping the run near the zero-penalty time region.

We have already achieved the maximum CRF, so use the remaining budget to confirm the local optimum boundary rather than risk repeating. Testing a slightly narrower upper bound checks whether the plateau extends lower in phi1 or whether 0.85 is the sharp optimum edge.

Now bracket the optimum in slope around the confirmed best phi window. A 12 min gradient will test whether the method sits on a broad CRF plateau or whether 14 min is truly the shortest program that preserves the critical 6–7 separation.

The 12 min version confirms loss of critical resolution, so test the opposite side of the slope optimum at the best phi window. This checks whether 14 min is the unique optimum or whether a slightly longer gradient maintains CRF = 1.000 as a robustness plateau.

The best point is established, so use the remaining injections to define how sensitive it is to window placement; raising phi0 one more step tests whether the lower bound can be trimmed further without harming early retention or the key 6–7 pair. This is the most relevant untested neighbor of the optimum.

Two methods now hit CRF 1.000, and the trend suggests higher phi0 may continue to shorten the run while keeping all peaks resolved. Testing phi0 = 0.20 maps the upper edge of this optimum plateau and checks whether the first peak is still safely retained rather than becoming effectively unretained.

The plateau extends to phi0 = 0.15 but degrades at 0.20, so test whether combining the successful higher phi0 with a slightly lower phi1 preserves the optimum. This maps the remaining untested corner adjacent to the two best methods and may identify another robust CRF 1.000 condition.

We have not yet tested the upper side of phi1 around the second CRF 1.000 plateau at phi0 = 0.15. This final local comparison will show whether 0.85 is the best upper bound there or whether the optimum remains broad toward 0.90.

The optimum plateau is centered at phi0 = 0.10–0.15, phi1 = 0.85, tG = 14, so the last useful test is whether the higher phi0 version tolerates a slightly steeper gradient better than the phi0 = 0.10 case. This defines the robustness boundary of the best family without repeating a method already run.
